The progression of a bond front hinges on... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/model-tracks-bond-front-velocity-for-wafer-and-die-bonding-imec/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/model-tracks-bond-front-velocity-for-wafer-and-die-bonding-imec/">Model Tracks Bond Front Velocity in Lubrication-Mediated Bonding of Flexible Substrates (imec)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>An imec researcher published a technical paper titled “Bond Front Velocity in Lubrication-Mediated Bonding of Flexible Substrates.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract:</strong></p>
<p>&#8220;Bonding and assembly processes have started to take the centre-stage in semiconductor manufacturing as they enable three-dimensional (3D) stacking and heterogeneous integration for novel interconnect architectures of integrated circuits. The progression of a bond front hinges on balance of adhesion and dissipation forces. Here, a lubrication–elasticity model is reported, to elucidate near-field dynamics of the process while staying within continuum limits, excluding adhesion mechanisms. When governed by lubrication flow in the gap, and linear elasticity in the substrates, the unbonded part of the substrates assumes a power-law shape as a function of the distance from the bond front. Furthermore, an entirely self-consistent formulation for the bond front velocity is derived. The formulation presented here crucially relies on a re-parameterization of the problem in terms of a ‘high viscous dissipation region’ ahead of the bond front, which travels along with the adhesion front. This approach for expressing the bond front velocity allows for its acceleration as the unbonded region shrinks, for example with bond front approaching the edge of a finite substrate. Finally, unifying velocity and length scales are proposed, incorporating a lateral adhesion front length scale that effectively captures velocity variations in the limit of vanishing viscous dissipation, bridging continuum and molecular scales. This framework provides scalable insights for better understanding and process control in applications with wafer and die bonding.&#8221;</p>
<p>Find the technical paper <a href="https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspa/article/482/2338/20260071/481833/Bond-front-velocity-in-lubrication-mediated">here</a>. May 2026.</p>
<p>Jain, Utkarsh. “Bond Front Velocity in Lubrication-Mediated Bonding of Flexible Substrates.” Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences 482, no. 2338 (2026): 20260071. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2026.0071.<br />
Creative Commons <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">license</a>.</p>

<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/rapid-switching-of-optical-properties-in-a-doped-semiconductor-by-femtosecond-laser-pulses-imperial-college-london-u-of-exeter/">Rapid Switching of Optical Properties in a Doped Semiconductor By Femtosecond Laser Pulses (Imperial College London, U. of Exeter)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers from Imperial College London and University of Exeter published a technical paper titled “Ultrafast switching of optical properties in a doped semiconductor by intense femtosecond laser pulses.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract </strong></p>
<p>&#8220;The rapid switching of materials when excited by ultrashort pulses of light is central for many optical technologies, and in particular to the developing field of time-varying metamaterials. These out-of-equilibrium interactions are difficult to capture with traditional theoretical models. Here we combine experiments and theory to unravel different regimes of interactions and a response saturation for a 44 fs, near-infrared pump pulse exciting a switchable doped semiconductor indium tin oxide thin film target. We model this process as a change in plasma frequency due to the excitation of hot electrons in a non-parabolic conduction band, which increases their effective mass. Our calculations show that saturation at high pump intensities arises because the pump heavily depopulates electrons from below the Fermi level. Excellent agreement with values extracted from experimental data confirms our model. For lower pump intensities, a two-temperature model is consistent with our data, but at higher intensities, it is apparent that other processes are at work, which we attribute to Auger transitions from the valence band, which introduce complex structure into the response, due to non-equilibrium rearrangement of energy between electrons and holes.&#8221;</p>
<p>Find the technical paper <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41377-026-02346-x">here</a>. August 2026.</p>
<p>Li, Yan, Stefano Vezzoli, Tim Klee, Joseph J. Broughton, Romain Tirole, Anthony C. Harwood, Hortense Allegre, et al. “Ultrafast Switching of Optical Properties in a Doped Semiconductor by Intense Femtosecond Laser Pulses.” Light: Science &amp; Applications 15, article 336 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-026-02346-x.</p>
<p>Creative Commons <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">license</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>SK hynix's $38B new fabs; memory density increases; 2026 chip industry revenue to hit $1.65T; imec metrology roadmap; MIT's self-assembled contacts; new U.S. restrictions; Intel's new training program; NXP to buy Ambarella?; AI sandbox leaks; memory-centric accelerator; entangled photons; CHIPS Act spending under scrutiny. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-150/">Chip Industry Week in Review</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<h3><strong>Memory/FMS</strong></h3>
<p>Denser, faster, and more distributed memory architectures for AI was the big news at the <strong>Future of Memory and Storage</strong> <a href="https://www.terrapinn.com/conference/future-memory-storage/">conference</a> this week:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Sandisk</strong> and <strong>SK hynix</strong> released the <a href="https://www.sandisk.com/company/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2026-08-03-Sandisk-and-sk-hynix-advance-global-standardization-of-hbf">High Bandwidth Flash</a> (HBF) spec, outlining basic performance expectations, the xPU-HBF host interface, and reliability and packaging guidance for an HBF die stack.</li>
<li><strong>Samsung</strong> showed concept models of <a href="https://semiconductor.samsung.com/news-events/news/samsung-unveils-next-gen-3d-memory-vision-at-fms-2026-charting-the-future-of-ai-infrastructure/">zHBM</a>, which vertically stacks HBM directly above AI accelerators, and zNAND-O, which vertically stacks multiple V-NAND chips through TSVs, as well as a 400+ layer BV-NAND using wafer bonding.</li>
<li><strong>Kioxia</strong> and <strong>Sandisk</strong> unveiled 10th-gen <a href="https://www.sandisk.com/company/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2026-08-04-new-3d-flash-memory-technology-from-kioxia-and-sandisk-qlc-nand">QLC 3D flash</a> memory technology, with bit density surpassing 37 Gb/mm² and a 4.8 Gb/s interface.</li>
<li><strong>NEO Semiconductor</strong> introduced a unified <a href="https://neosemic.com/neo-semiconductor-launches-neo-ai-memory-platform-to-solve-ais-two-biggest-memory-bottlenecks/">AI memory platform</a> that combines SRAM with higher on-chip memory density, as well as 3D DRAM that uses 3D NAND manufacturing processes to increase HBM capacity.</li>
<li><strong>SK hynix</strong> is developing 375-layer <a href="https://news.skhynix.com/en/hbf-at-fms-2026/">4D NAND</a>. Find SK&#8217;s AI memory roadmap <a href="https://news.skhynix.com/en/fms-2026/">here</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Marvell</strong> announced a <a href="https://www.marvell.com/company/newsroom/marvell-ai-memory-infrastructure-agentic-ai-inference.html">PCIe 6.0 SSD controller</a> for servers, rack-level memory expansion and pooling solutions, and a multi-rack optical shared-memory architecture for AI inference.</li>
<li>Find more FMS news in the <a href="#New Technologies">New Technologies</a> section below.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Capacity</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>SK hynix</strong> approved about $38B in new spending for its <a href="https://news.skhynix.com/en/fab-facility-investment-2026/">Yongin Y2 and Cheongju M17 fabs</a>, advancing previously announced capacity expansions for HBM, DRAM and NAND.</li>
<li><strong>SpaceX</strong> and <strong>Tesla</strong> provided new details for their previously announced <a href="https://www.spacex.com/updates">Terafab semiconductor project</a> in Grimes County, Texas, reporting a $16.8B initial phase, a planned 100 million s.f. complex, and at least 3,000 jobs. The vertically integrated facility is intended to manufacture, package, and test AI chips for Tesla vehicles and robots and SpaceX compute systems.</li>
<li><strong>CXMT</strong> is reportedly considering a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/cxmt-plans-second-chip-plant-beijing-is-talks-its-funding-sources-say-2026-08-03/">second memory plant</a> in Beijing.</li>
<li><strong>Silicon Box</strong> said will <a href="https://www.silicon-box.com/silicon-box-ships-500m-units-at-high-yield-expands-production-capacity-for-panel-level-packaging">increase advanced packaging capacity</a> by 10X this year.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Big money</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>AMD</strong> is <a href="https://ir.amd.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1296/amd-acquires-taalas-to-advance-compute-solutions-for-rapidly-growing-ai-inference-market">acquiring</a> <strong>Taalas</strong>, a Toronto startup developing specialized AI-inference silicon. Terms were not disclosed.</li>
<li><strong>NXP </strong>is in talks to buy <strong>Ambarella</strong>, a chipmaker valued at over $3B, reports <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/f02ce02b-fa33-49ad-b8c7-81ab5cec3de0?syn-25a6b1a6=1">The Financial Times.</a></li>
<li><strong>Lumilens</strong> emerged from stealth with $900M to make co-packaged, near-packaged, and pluggable <a href="https://lumilens.com/news-insights/lumilens-emerges-with-900m-in-funding">optical interconnects</a>.</li>
<li><strong>OLIX</strong> raised $312M to develop an <a href="https://olix.com/news/company-raises-series-b">AI platform</a> that uses specialized chips for each stage of the token production process.</li>
<li><strong>SiEngine</strong> raised $200M for its in-cabin and <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/ecarx-backed-chip-maker-siengine-secures-us200m-equity-financing-to-accelerate-vertical-silicon-to-software-sdv-innovation-302839948.html">ADAS SoCs</a> for software-defined vehicles.</li>
<li><strong>Acrab</strong> raised $130M for its <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/acrab-raises-us130-million-series-b-advancing-agentic-ai-compute-platform-commercialization-302844535.html">agentic AI</a> platform that combines edge silicon, models, and SW orchestration.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Industry Growth</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>WSTS</strong> reports the worldwide semiconductor <a href="https://www.wsts.org/esraCMS/extension/media/f/WST/7734/WSTS-Q2-Release-2026-08-06.pdf">market hit $702B</a> in the first half of 2026, a 102% increase year-over-year, with memory up 305% and logic up 45%. The organization predicts full-year revenue will hit nearly $1.65T. Also, see <strong>SIA&#8217;</strong>s June and Q2 report <a href="https://www.semiconductors.org/global-semiconductor-sales-increase-35-1-from-q1-2026-to-q2-2026/">here</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h3 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>Metrology Roadmap</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li style="text-align: left;" role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>Imec’s</strong> latest <a href="https://www.imec-int.com/en/articles/four-decades-fab-metrology-and-inspection-pivotal-milestones-and-road-ahead">metrology roadmap</a> calls for higher-energy e-beam tools, shorter-wavelength optical systems, and X-rays that probe deeper into silicon, supported by multi-e-beam inspection, multi-head AFM, AI denoising, and virtual metrology.</li>
</ul>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24279628 size-full" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Revised-Metrology-and-inspection-roadmap-copy-2.jpeg?resize=1200%2C640&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1200" height="640" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Revised-Metrology-and-inspection-roadmap-copy-2.jpeg?w=1200&amp;ssl=1 1200w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Revised-Metrology-and-inspection-roadmap-copy-2.jpeg?resize=300%2C160&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Revised-Metrology-and-inspection-roadmap-copy-2.jpeg?resize=1024%2C546&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Revised-Metrology-and-inspection-roadmap-copy-2.jpeg?resize=768%2C410&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Revised-Metrology-and-inspection-roadmap-copy-2.jpeg?resize=600%2C320&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />

<h3><strong>U.S. government</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>The Dept. of Commerce canceled or paused several original CHIPS R&amp;D awards and is redirecting some funding into individual company investments, but the <strong>Government Accountability Office</strong> says it has not clearly explained <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-109121">how those investments will fulfill</a> the national research and advanced-packaging programs required by Congress.</li>
<li>The U.S. government announced a minimum import <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/adjusting-imports-of-polysilicon-and-its-derivatives-into-the-united-states/">price program and a 15% duty on polysilicon</a>-derived products, effective Dec. 4, aimed at countering Chinese competition for the material used in IC and solar manufacturing supply chains.</li>
<li>The FCC is considering blocking imports of new <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/trump-administration-drafting-ban-chinese-data-center-devices-sources-say-2026-08-04/">Chinese optical transceivers</a>, as a protective measure for U.S. data centers.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Security</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>No matter how AI-savvy an engineering team may be, sandbox escapes involving <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals">Anthropic</a>, <a href="https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/">OpenAI</a>, and <a href="https://securityaffairs.com/196731/security/meta-ai-model-hacked-a-company-during-testing-marking-third-ai-lab-incident.html">Meta</a> are raising everyone’s blood pressure. For the IC industry, security no longer can be treated as a separate step. It must be integrated across <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-friend-and-foe-for-security/">chip design, manufacturing, and the broader lifecycle</a>, changing both the priority and sequence in which vulnerabilities are addressed. Seven experts explain why security must be <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-next-big-chip-failure-may-be-a-security-one/">built into designs</a> from the earliest stages of the flow. The threat even extends into space. As NASA brings internet connectivity to astronauts, rovers, and orbiters, <a href="https://semiengineering.com/as-space-gets-connected-security-gets-critical/">a growing network of high-value data</a> could become a target for ransomware groups and hostile nations.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Notable research</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>U. of Michigan</strong> researchers designed a <a href="https://news.engin.umich.edu/2026/08/designing-memory-centric-chips-for-future-space-telescopes/">memory-centric accelerator</a> that splits the data and processing across 56 custom chiplets, each with about 2 GB of distributed SRAM, potentially cutting space-telescope image-processing power from 3,000W to as little as 51W.</li>
<li><strong>MIT</strong> researchers created a two-step fabrication method that adds fragile molecular layers after conventional chip processing, then uses capillary and van der Waals forces to <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-026-02227-9">self-assemble damage-free metal contacts</a>. The team built more than 1,000 devices with sub-1nm molecular layers, achieving a 96% average yield and stable operation over tens of thousands of electrical cycles, including an interconnected molecular-memory array.</li>
<li><strong>D-Wave</strong> demonstrated &#8220;a fast, <a href="https://www.dwavequantum.com/company/newsroom/press-release/d-wave-demonstrates-major-hardware-breakthrough-for-quantum-error-correction/">high-fidelity, two-qubit entangling gate</a> that preserves the error-correction advantages of D-Wave’s superconducting dual-rail qubit architecture.&#8221; The company says the work enables &#8220;a faster path to error-corrected systems that rapidly suppress errors as they scale.&#8221;</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="New Technologies"><strong>New Technologies</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Bruker</strong> introduced two <a href="https://www.bruker.com/en/news-and-events/news/2026/bruker-announces-major-advances-in-detector-technology-for-semiconductor-thin-film-energy-materials-and-nanostructure-characterization.html">SEM detectors for faster, higher-resolution materials analysis</a>. The eWARP TKD provides sub-2nm crystallographic mapping at up to 5,700 frames per second, while the XFlash FlatQUAD 2L simultaneously collects elemental EDS data and BSE images.</p>
<p><strong>ams OSRAM</strong> has begun developing <a href="https://ams-osram.com/news/press-releases/q2-2026-results">micro-photodiode arrays for the receiver side</a> of high-bandwidth optical interconnects in AI data centers, extending its optical-semiconductor roadmap beyond microLED transmitters.</p>
<p><strong>Anthropic</strong> plans to design ​<a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/anthropic-build-in-house-chip-design-team-claude-hire-engineers-2026-08-05/">custom chips</a> for its AI models, per Reuters.</p>

<h2 id="Research"><strong>Research</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Imperial College London</strong> and <strong>University of Exeter</strong> researchers demonstrated &#8220;<a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41377-026-02346-x">ultrafast switching of optical properties in a doped semiconductor</a> by intense femtosecond laser pulses.&#8221;</p>
<p>In a step toward bringing 6G devices closer to reality, a team at <strong>Science Tokyo</strong> created an integrated <a href="https://www.isct.ac.jp/en/news/sky36rjhic8h">phased-array wireless circuit</a> with &#8220;144 Gbps dual-polarized MIMO communication in the 150 GHz sub-terahertz band.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>MIT</strong> and <strong>Argonne</strong> researchers developed a way to <a href="https://news.mit.edu/2026/new-way-watch-heat-move-through-electronics-0806">map heat flow inside multilayer semiconductor devices</a> using ultrafast X-ray diffraction and laser heating. In a GaN-on-silicon structure, they found that a micron-scale wrinkle reduced local heat transfer fourfold and cut heat flow across the interface by 25%, providing a new method for locating thermal bottlenecks in advanced chips.</p>
<p><strong>UCSD</strong> developed an <a href="https://today.ucsd.edu/story/insect-inspired-electronic-nose-turning-semiconductor-chips-into-olfactory-sensors">electronic nose with graphene FETs</a> and an integrated wearable <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-75980-z">smart ring for biochemical monitoring</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Looking for more?</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Handbook of <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11484">Error-Correcting Codes</a> (<strong>NIST, Freie Universität Berlin</strong>)</li>
<li><a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41578-026-00949-9">Engineered interfaces</a> in materials for energy-efficient computing (<strong>Berkeley)</strong></li>
<li>Surface smoothing of monocrystalline <a href="https://pubs.aip.org/avs/jva/article/44/4/042601/3396164/Rapid-surface-smoothing-of-monocrystalline-diamond">diamond w/bias-pulsed ALE</a> (<strong>UIUC</strong> et al.)</li>
<li>Inter-Chiplet End-to-End PHY Modeling for <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24221">Accurate Chiplet Simulation</a> (<strong>Uppsala</strong>)</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2 id="Security"><strong>Security</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Government intervention</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Attorneys general from 15 U.S. states sent a letter to <strong>OpenAI </strong>calling for company leaders to <a href="https://www.iowaattorneygeneral.gov/media/cms/08_5392C9E17791C.pdf">preserve evidence</a> related to last month’s exposure of Hugging Face data.</li>
<li>The state of New York is giving $9M to municipal water authorities across the state to improve their cybersecurity infrastructure after a wave of <a href="https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/governor-hochul-announces-more-9-million-cybersecurity-grants-help-protect-153-water-systems">recent cyberattacks on local water systems</a> around the country.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Alerts and attacks</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Nvidia</strong> issued critical/high level alerts on Dynamo for Linux for an <a href="https://nvidia.custhelp.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/5842">out-of bounds write vulnerability</a>.</li>
<li><strong>AMD</strong> warned that precisely timed interrupts may weaken Linux’s Safe RET mitigation on Zen 1 and 2 processors, potentially exposing data through <a href="https://www.amd.com/en/resources/product-security/bulletin/amd-sb-7061.html">speculative execution</a>. The chipmaker also issued alerts on <a href="https://www.amd.com/en/resources/product-security/bulletin/amd-sb-7068.html">memory aliasing</a> and <a href="https://www.amd.com/en/resources/product-security/bulletin/amd-sb-9027.html">auto updater</a> vulnerabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Cisco</strong> reported a vulnerability in the web-based management interface of its <a href="https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cimc-arg-inject-upSHdMfU">Integrated Management Controller</a>.</li>
<li>Researchers at <strong>VulnCheck </strong>said they uncovered a <a href="https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/zbt-endlessdoors">backdoor built into dozens of Chinese-made internet router models</a> that give a Chinese server full control over the router.</li>
<li><strong>IBM</strong> found that 25% of malicious data breaches involved AI, with an <a href="https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-07-29-ibm-study-one-in-four-malicious-breaches-are-ai-enabled,-costing-companies-6-million-on-average">average breach cost of $6M</a>, while companies using AI-powered security tools reduced costs by nearly $2M.</li>
<li><strong>CISA</strong>’s alerts for the week are <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories">here.</a></li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Guidance, incident report</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>The UK’s <strong>AI Security Institute</strong> released an incident report on more unsanctioned activities against “<a href="https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/incident-report-unsanctioned-agent-behaviour-during-cyber-testing">real people and organizations</a>” by <strong>OpenAI </strong>and <strong>Anthropic</strong> AI agents during cyber testing.</li>
<li><strong>Intel</strong> published new analysis of <a href="https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/security/security-practices/blogs/rowhammer-whose-issue-to-mitigate.html">Rowhammer mitigation best practices</a>, reviewing the lessons learned since the attacks first emerged.</li>
<li><strong>Microsoft</strong> released <a href="https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/advance-zero-trust-for-ai-new-tools-and-guidance-to-secure-ai-agents-and-devsecops/">new cybersecurity tools and guidance</a> to support organizations defending against AI threats.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>New security tools</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>French cybersecurity developer <strong>Thales</strong> released a new hardware security module built to provide <a href="https://www.thalesgroup.com/en/news-centre/press-releases/thales-builds-cryptographic-security-age-ai-and-post-quantum-computing">quantum-resistant security</a>, including PKI, certificate management, authentication, digital signing and identities.</li>
<li><strong>3mdeb </strong>launched <a href="https://blog.3mdeb.com/2026/2026-07-30-msi-pro-b850p-v090-release/">open-source firmware</a> for <strong>AMD</strong>&#8216;s Ryzen desktop platform.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Cybersecurity tech papers and analysis</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Watermarking for <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05055">Physical Design IP Protection</a> (<strong>UCSD</strong>)</li>
<li>Demystifying <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28233">DRAM Read Disturbance</a> (<strong>ETH Zurich</strong> et al.)</li>

<li>Challenges in <a href="https://www.iaps.ai/research/the-openaihugging-face-incident-challenges-in-controlling-and-containing-cyber-capable-ai-systems">Controlling/Containing Cyber-Capable AI Systems</a> (<strong>IAPS</strong>)</li>

<h2 id="Vehicles, Batteries"><strong>Vehicles, Batteries</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>New Auto Tech</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Infineon</strong> is partnering with <strong>MediaTek </strong>on advanced AI-driven <a href="https://www.infineon.com/technology-news/2026/inftn202608-127">in-cabin experience tech for future vehicles</a>, with MediaTek qualifying the Infineon 512 Mb Quad SPI NOR flash for use in its Dimensity Auto Cockpit platform C-X1.</li>
<li><strong>BMW</strong> will start outfitting its fleet vehicles with <strong>NXP&#8217;s</strong> <a href="https://www.nxp.com/company/about-nxp/newsroom/NW-UWB-POWERS-BMW-KEY-PRESENCE">Trimension Ultra-Wideband ranging and radar technology</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Vehicle security</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Upstream Security</strong>’s new report on automotive and smart mobility cybersecurity found that <a href="https://upstream.auto/reports/global-automotive-cybersecurity-report/">automotive ransom attacks</a> more than doubled last year compared to 2024.</li>
<li><strong>CISA</strong> disclosed a hard-coded cryptographic key in <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-216-01">Acrisure KARR BT and DR-100 vehicle anti-theft systems</a> that could allow an attacker within Bluetooth range to issue unauthorized vehicle-control commands.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>EVs &amp; AVs</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>The <a href="https://www.yolegroup.com/press-release/power-chip-market-for-xevs-to-hit-14-5-billion-by-2031/">power chip market for xEVs</a> is expected to hit $14.5B by 2031, according to research published by <strong>Yole Group</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Ford </strong>announced that its new mid-sized <a href="https://www.ford.com/electric/fathom/?srsltid=AfmBOoq8q-T8W2_Hkhbo5bor8Gi8v7_D5IfGApnzRgq7EYW7SRLc_HGm">electric pickup truck</a> will be called the “Fathom” and have a starting price of just over $28K.</li>
<li><strong>Mercedes-Benz </strong>debuted its new <a href="https://media.mbusa.com/releases/release-6ca53c576cbfe9c8df2badfd0e0052a0-mercedes-amg-gt-53-4-door-coupe-powerful-entry-into-the-new-gt-series">AMG GT 53</a>, an electric sports car with ~500 miles of range, expected to hit the U.S. market next year.</li>
<li>The California Teamsters union is suing multiple California government agencies over the state’s new rules guiding the <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/teamsters-california-sues-dmv-to-protect-public-from-driverless-truck-dangers-302844270.html">rollout of autonomous trucking</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Lucid Motors</strong> is <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/lucid-plans-save-14-billion-2026-cost-cuts-losses-mount-2026-08-04/">pushing back</a> the release of its anticipated electric crossover-SUV by about a year amid major <a href="https://media.lucidmotors.com/article?id=3rj6dmTlMFKBar2joT1PMw">cost-cutting efforts</a>, with the vehicle now expected to hit the market in the second half of 2027.</li>
<li>Indian electric two-wheeler manufacturer <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-simple-energy/">Simple Energy<strong>,</strong></a> cardiovascular medical device manufacturer <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-sahajanand-medical-technologies/">Sahajanand Medical</a> and electric air taxi developer <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-sarla-aviation/">Sarla Aviation</a> all expanded their adoption of <strong>Siemens</strong>’ cloud-based software solutions.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Trending Video"><strong>Trending Video</strong></h2>
<p><a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-agent-orchestration-for-asic-autonomy/">AI Agent Orchestration For ASIC Autonomy</a>: The use of AI agents in chip design has been limited to small portions of the design flow. Engineers have been proceeding cautiously to understand how agents work, how to ensure they are delivering consistent results, and how different agents work together. The next step is to extend their role beyond just gluing together coding and tooling functions. Mehir Arora, head of engineering at <strong>ChipAgents</strong>, explains what happens when the role of AI agents is expanded to include semantics and physics, what happens when agents work in parallel on different engineering problems, and what’s needed to achieve a 10X or greater improvement in productivity.<br />
<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/WMKiQUYQhnA" width="480" height="270" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="allowfullscreen">&lt;/ifram</iframe></p>

<h2 id="Quantum"><strong>Quantum</strong></h2>
<p><strong>NIST</strong> researchers and collaborators demonstrated a <a href="https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/08/spooky-particles-transit-dc-suburbs-step-toward-quantum-network">quantum network</a> by sending entangled photons through 62 kilometers (~38.5 miles) of commercial fiber in Maryland.</p>
<p><strong>QuiX </strong>released a rack-mountable <a href="https://www.quixquantum.com/news/quix-quantum-launches-alquor-2">quantum silicon nitride photonic</a> processor platform in 8-mode, 20-mode and 32-mode configurations for quantum optics research.</p>
<p><strong>IonQ</strong> will spend $15M over 5 years on a quantum communication <a href="https://www.ionq.com/news/ionq-and-epb-partner-to-launch-the-tennessee-quantum-communications-research-center">R&amp;D lab</a> in Tennessee.</p>
<p><strong>OptQC</strong> and <strong>NTT</strong> will team up to build a fault-tolerant, 1 million-qubit-class <a href="https://www.optqc.com/en/news/news/optqc-ntt-2026">optical quantum</a> computer.</p>
<p>A new <strong>DARPA</strong> program aims to establish a pilot manufacturing pipeline for tactical-grade <a href="https://www.darpa.mil/news/2026/its-about-time">optical clocks</a>.</p>
<h3><strong>Quantum tech papers</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Air-stable, <a href="https://news.mit.edu/2026/researchers-make-air-stable-ultrathin-superconductors-more-scalable-quantum-devices-0805">ultrathin superconductors</a>, for more scalable quantum devices (<strong>MIT)</strong></li>
<li><a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s44335-026-00085-1">Cryogenic HW accelerator for quantum</a> state discrimination @4K (<strong>Berkeley Lab)</strong></li>
<li>Closed Timelike Curve <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27473">Decoding on Quantum HW</a> (<strong>U Mass, Stony Brook</strong>)</li>
<li>Resource Estimation for <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04573">Fault-Tolerant Quantum</a> Programs (<strong>Tsinghua, Sydney</strong>)</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Workforce, Education"><strong>Workforce, Education</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Intel</strong> launched the <a href="https://newsroom.intel.com/corporate/creating-pathways-to-semiconductor-careers-intel-launches-sepp">Semiconductor Education Pathways Program</a> (SEPP), funding K-12, community college and university programs in Arizona, New Mexico, Ohio and Oregon to expand semiconductor workforce pipelines through hands-on training, curriculum and faculty development, and scholarships and fellowships.</p>
<p><strong>SEMI University</strong> has several upcoming <a href="https://www.semi.org/en/semi-university/course-calendar">August training courses</a>, including &#8220;Inside the Fab&#8221; for Asia/EU on <strong data-start="1680" data-end="1694">Aug. 17–20</strong>, semiconductor technology/business for the Americas on <strong data-start="1750" data-end="1761">Aug. 18</strong>, and &#8220;Overview of Semiconductor Manufacturing&#8221; on <strong data-start="1810" data-end="1824">Aug. 19–20</strong>.</p>
<p><strong>University of Florida&#8217;s</strong> Semiconductor Institute is encouraging educators to start a <a href="https://fsi.institute.ufl.edu/semi-clubs/">SemiClub</a>, an initiative giving K-12 students hands-on activities, seminars, field trips, and career exploration focused on <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KzdW96kbZTo">semiconductors and microelectronics</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Oregon State University</strong> is churning out <a href="https://today.oregonstate.edu/all-stories/discovery-industry-oregon-state-spinouts-are-building-future-semiconductors">semiconductor spinouts</a>. The technologies include <strong>Amorphyx</strong>&#8216;s amorphous metal transistors,<strong> Inpria&#8217;s</strong> metal oxide photoresists, <strong>NexTC&#8217;s</strong> thin-film coating processes, <strong>Phosio&#8217;s</strong> materials for smart glasses/displays, and <strong>Valliscor&#8217;s</strong> domestically produced fluorinated etchant gases.</p>
<p><strong>Warning</strong>: Employers are experiencing growing numbers of <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-30/fake-job-applications-are-becoming-a-hiring-problem">fraudulent job applicants</a> using stolen identities, AI-generated résumés and deepfakes, leading recruiters to tighten identity and background checks, reports Bloomberg. An Equifax survey found that <a href="https://investor.equifax.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1415/equifax-survey-three-in-four-hr-professionals-report">3 out of 4</a> HR professionals found challenges with fabricated/misleading applicant info.</p>
<h3><strong>More educational offerings</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Virginia Tech</strong> is opening an <a href="https://news.vt.edu/articles/2026/08/NSF-grant-semiconductor-lab.html">AI-enabled cloud-based semiconductor laboratory</a>.</li>
<li><strong>UT Austin</strong> now has a B.S. in <a href="https://news.utexas.edu/2026/08/03/ut-launches-new-materials-science-bachelors-program/">Materials Science and Engineering</a> program.</li>
</ul>

		<title>Separating The Chaff From The Wheat: Focusing On Only The RDC Violations You Care About</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/separating-the-chaff-from-the-wheat-focusing-on-only-the-rdc-violations-you-care-about/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/separating-the-chaff-from-the-wheat-focusing-on-only-the-rdc-violations-you-care-about/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Reetika]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:07:57 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Building The IoE]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[metastability]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[RDC]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[reset domain crossing]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[resets]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Siemens EDA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[verification]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24279646</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Combine structural analysis with timing awareness and context-based classification to distinguish real design risks from safe implementation choices.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/separating-the-chaff-from-the-wheat-focusing-on-only-the-rdc-violations-you-care-about/">Separating The Chaff From The Wheat: Focusing On Only The RDC Violations You Care About</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Modern system-on-chips (SoCs) are no longer built around a single clock and a single reset. Today&#8217;s designs integrate hundreds of IP blocks, multiple power domains, software-controlled reset sequences, and sophisticated power-management techniques. While these advancements have enabled remarkable functionality and performance, they have also introduced new verification challenges—one of the most significant being reset domain crossing (RDC) verification.</p>
<p>RDC verification has become an essential part of design sign-off because it identifies situations where different reset domains interact in ways that may lead to metastability or functional failures. However, as SoCs continue to grow in complexity, another challenge has become increasingly apparent: verification noise. Many engineering teams spend more time investigating RDC violations that are actually safe than fixing genuine design issues. The question is no longer simply, &#8220;Can we detect RDC violations?&#8221; The more important question is, &#8220;Can we distinguish genuine design risks from safe implementation choices?&#8221;</p>
<h2>Why conventional RDC verification produces so many violations</h2>
<p>Traditional RDC verification relies primarily on structural analysis. If two sequential elements belong to different reset domains, the crossing is reported as a potential RDC violation. From a safety perspective, this conservative approach is justified. Different reset domains may assert or de-assert independently, potentially allowing unstable values to propagate through the design. Reporting every possible interaction minimizes the likelihood of missing a genuine bug. The limitation, however, is that structural analysis alone does not capture the designer&#8217;s intent.</p>
<p>Today’s SoCs often employ sophisticated reset architectures involving reset controllers, synchronized reset generation, staged initialization sequences, and software-controlled resets. These mechanisms intentionally create multiple reset domains while still ensuring correct functional behavior.</p>
<p>Consequently, many structurally different reset crossings do not present any real metastability risk. Yet conventional RDC analysis reports them all as violations, leaving engineers to manually separate true failures from safe implementations. For large designs, this often results in thousands—or even tens of thousands—of reported violations, significantly increasing debug effort and slowing verification closure.</p>
<h2>Different reset domains do not always mean different risks</h2>
<p>One of the most common misconceptions in RDC verification is assuming that different reset domains automatically imply metastability. In reality, the safety of a crossing depends on <strong>how resets are generated and how they interact with the clock</strong>, not simply on whether two registers belong to different reset domains.</p>
<p>Consider a design in which both the transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) registers operate on the same clock but belong to different asynchronous reset domains. At first glance, this appears to be a typical RDC violation.</p>
<p>Now consider that the transmitter reset is itself generated synchronously within that clock domain using a reset-generation register. Because the reset transition is synchronized to the clock, any reset-induced transition at the transmitter occurs only on a clock edge. Consequently, the receiver also observes only clock-aligned transitions.</p>
<p>In this situation, the crossing behaves as a conventional synchronous timing path rather than an asynchronous RDC hazard. If static timing analysis (STA) confirms that setup and hold requirements are satisfied, the implementation is functionally safe.</p>
<p>Structurally, the path appears to cross different reset domains. Functionally, it behaves like a correctly timed synchronous path. Nevertheless, conventional RDC verification continues to report it as a violation because it considers only reset-domain differences rather than the underlying design behavior.</p>
<p>Figure 1 illustrates the difference between conventional structural RDC analysis and the proposed STA-aware methodology. Instead of reporting every reset-domain crossing as a functional violation, the enhanced flow identifies crossings that are timing-safe and classifies them separately for STA validation.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279647" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?resize=622%2C434&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="622" height="434" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?w=622&amp;ssl=1 622w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C209&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Siemens_Separating-Chaff-from-Wheat-RDC-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C419&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 622px) 100vw, 622px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Flow of RDC analysis.</strong></p>
<h2>The same principle applies to other RDC scenarios</h2>
<p>This concept extends beyond crossings between asynchronous reset domains. For example, designers frequently encounter crossings where the transmitter belongs to an asynchronous reset domain while the receiver has no reset at all. Conventional RDC tools classify these paths as violations because a non-resettable register effectively belongs to its own reset domain. However, if the transmitter reset is generated synchronously within the same clock domain, the receiver still observes only clock-synchronous transitions. In this case, timing—not reset behavior—determines correctness.</p>
<p>Another common example involves crossings from an asynchronous reset domain to a synchronous reset domain. Structural analysis reports these as potential RDC violations because the reset types differ. In practice, if reset sequencing guarantees that the receiver is already held in reset whenever the transmitter resets, and STA validates the timing path, the crossing does not introduce a functional RDC hazard.</p>
<h2>Bringing context into RDC verification</h2>
<p>Instead of asking only whether two registers belong to different reset domains, context-aware RDC verification asks a more meaningful question: Does this crossing actually create a metastability risk, or is it simply a timing path that should be validated through STA?</p>
<p>This seemingly small shift fundamentally changes the verification process. Rather than reporting every structurally different reset interaction as a violation, the verification flow evaluates additional design context, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>How the reset is generated</li>
<li>Whether the reset source is synchronous to the operating clock</li>
<li>Whether the transmitter and receiver share the same clock domain</li>
<li>Whether the path can be safely validated through STA</li>
</ul>
<p>When these conditions indicate that the crossing is functionally safe, the path is no longer reported as a functional RDC violation. Instead, it is classified as an <strong>STA-aware caution</strong>, indicating that the crossing requires timing validation rather than RDC debugging. This additional context allows engineers to focus on genuine functional issues while ensuring that timing-related paths are still verified through the appropriate analysis methodology.</p>
<h2>Better classification—not fewer checks</h2>
<p>A common misconception is that reducing reported violations means relaxing verification. That is not the objective. The goal is <strong>better classification</strong>. True RDC hazards continue to be reported exactly as before. Only crossings that can be demonstrated to be timing-safe through reset behavior and design context are separated from genuine functional RDC failures.</p>
<p>This distinction enables verification engineers to prioritize their efforts more effectively by distinguishing between:</p>
<ul>
<li>Genuine RDC failures requiring functional investigation</li>
<li>Timing-safe crossings requiring STA validation</li>
<li>Safe implementation choices that do not require further RDC debugging</li>
</ul>
<p>This methodology reduces false positives without compromising verification quality or sign-off confidence.</p>
<h2>Measuring the impact</h2>
<p>To evaluate this methodology, it was applied to a large industrial design containing nearly 296,000 register bits, multiple memories, and several latch-based elements.</p>
<p>Conventional RDC verification reported approximately 50,000 RDC violations. A significant portion of these represented crossings that were structurally different but functionally safe.</p>
<p>By incorporating STA-aware classification, approximately 10,000 crossings were automatically identified as timing-safe and reclassified as cautions instead of violations.</p>
<p>The resulting improvements included:</p>
<table style="border-collapse: collapse;" border="1">
<thead>
<tr style="background-color: #ddd;">
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Metric</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Result</strong></td>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Total reported RDC violations</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">~50,000</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Crossings reclassified as STA-aware cautions</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">~10,000</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Reduction in reported violations</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Nearly 20%</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">False positives</td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Verification closure</td>

</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Most importantly, all genuine RDC hazards remained visible throughout the verification process. The methodology reduced verification noise—not verification quality.</p>
<h2>Looking ahead</h2>
<p>Simply identifying every possible reset interaction is no longer sufficient. Verification tools must also understand the design context and distinguish structural differences from genuine functional risks.</p>
<p>By combining traditional RDC analysis with timing awareness and context-based classification, engineers can significantly reduce false positives while maintaining the confidence required for silicon sign-off. The result is not fewer checks, but more meaningful insights—allowing engineering teams to focus their time on solving real design problems instead of investigating safe reset crossings.</p>
<p>To learn more about the methodology, kindly download the full paper <a href="https://resources.sw.siemens.com/en-US/white-paper-from-false-alarms-to-real-insights-refining-rdc-to-catch-missed-sta-scenarios/">Refining RDC to catch missed STA scenarios</a>.</p>

		<title>Shared IDE For PCIe Bifurcation: Scaling Security Without Scaling Complexity &#038; Resources</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Vincent van der Leest]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:06:17 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Security Matters]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[data in motion]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PCIe]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Rambus]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[security]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24279641</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Allowing multiple controllers and links to utilize a common security infrastructure while maintaining independent protection mechanisms.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/">Shared IDE For PCIe Bifurcation: Scaling Security Without Scaling Complexity &#038; Resources</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>PCIe is the primary high-speed interconnect used to connect processors with accelerators, memory devices, storage, and networking components. It provides a common and scalable foundation for moving large volumes of data between the compute and I/O resources that make up a modern system. As architectures add more powerful accelerators and higher-performance devices, PCIe continues to evolve to deliver greater bandwidth while maintaining low latency and broad ecosystem interoperability. These capabilities have made it essential to data center, AI, cloud, networking, storage, and other performance-intensive systems.</p>
<h2>PCIe security is no longer optional</h2>
<p>As PCIe links carry increasingly sensitive workloads, protecting data in motion has become as important as bandwidth, latency, and interoperability. Data moving between processors, accelerators, memory devices, storage subsystems, and network adapters must be protected against interception, tampering, and replay attacks, particularly in AI training, confidential computing, cloud infrastructure, and high-performance data processing.</p>
<p>The PCIe specification defines Integrity and Data Encryption (IDE) as the standard for securing data across a PCIe link. IDE protects Transaction Layer Packets with confidentiality, integrity, and replay protection as they travel between connected components.</p>
<h2>Bifurcation is becoming more common</h2>
<p>A growing trend to support more devices and make better use of available lanes is PCIe bifurcation, which divides a single wider interface into multiple independent links. For example, a PCIe x16 interface can be configured as two x8 links, four x4 links, or a combination such as x8 + x4 + x2 + x2. The total lane count remains unchanged, but those lanes form more independent connections.</p>
<p>Bifurcation gives system designers greater flexibility, improves lane utilization, supports multiple endpoints, and enables reduced resource usage. That flexibility also changes the security model: one x16 link is not equivalent to four separate links because each independent connection requires its own IDE protection, as illustrated in the figure below.</p>
<p>This creates an implementation challenge for traditional architectures, which typically dedicate IDE resources to each PCIe controller or port. As the number of independent links grows, designers may need additional encryption engines and management logic, increasing silicon area, power, and design complexity.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279642" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=1948%2C791&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1948" height="791" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?w=1948&amp;ssl=1 1948w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C122&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C416&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C312&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=1536%2C624&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C244&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<h2>Why traditional IDE architectures become inefficient</h2>
<p>With bifurcation increasing the number of links, designers often find themselves replicating encryption engines, management logic, and supporting security infrastructure. This approach introduces several challenges, such as:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Area growth: </strong>Each additional protected link requires additional hardware resources. As the number of links scales, area consumption can grow significantly.</li>
<li><strong>Floorplanning complexity: </strong>Security logic must often be placed close to individual controllers, creating congestion and making physical implementation more difficult.</li>
<li><strong>Scalability limitations: </strong>Security resources scale in proportion to controller count rather than actual throughput requirements. This can produce inefficiencies in highly bifurcated designs.</li>
</ul>
<p>The result is an architecture where security becomes a scaling bottleneck. Designers gain flexibility through bifurcation but pay for it through duplicated security hardware.</p>
<h2>Enter Shared IDE</h2>
<p>Shared IDE takes a different approach. Instead of duplicating IDE resources for every PCIe controller, Shared IDE (as shown in the earlier diagram) allows multiple controllers and links to utilize a common security infrastructure while maintaining independent protection mechanisms.</p>
<p>This fundamentally changes the scaling model. Rather than tying security resource growth directly to the number of ports, Shared IDE enables security resources to be shared across multiple interfaces, reducing duplication without compromising standards compliance.</p>
<p>The approach offers three primary benefits:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Lower cost and area: </strong>By eliminating unnecessary duplication, Shared IDE can reduce overall hardware requirements. This leads to fewer replicated security blocks, lower silicon area, and improved power efficiency.</li>
<li><strong>Greater design flexibility: </strong>Shared IDE can be physically separated from PCIe controllers and PHYs, giving implementation teams more freedom during floorplanning, which helps to reduce congestion and facilitates easier timing closure.</li>
<li><strong>Security without compromise: </strong>Importantly, sharing resources does not mean sharing security contexts. Each port retains independent protection, dedicated security contexts, separate key management, and standards-aligned PCIe IDE compliance. This means security remains isolated even while implementation resources are shared.</li>
</ul>
<p>Therefore, the shared infrastructure performs common processing tasks while preserving logical separation between protected connections. In other words, a good Shared IDE implementation reduces overhead without reducing trust.</p>
<p>The concept is specifically developed so that security scaling becomes independent of controller scaling. This distinction is important because future PCIe systems are expected to continue increasing both performance and connectivity. Security architectures that depend on linear duplication will become increasingly difficult to justify from both cost and implementation complexity perspectives.</p>
<h2>Shared IDE for high-performance PCIe</h2>
<p>Rambus has implemented this Shared IDE approach in a production-ready architecture designed specifically for high-performance PCIe systems. The Rambus Shared IDE solution enables multiple PCIe controllers and links to use a common security infrastructure while maintaining an independent security context for each port. Because PCIe traffic is packetized, the architecture can arbitrate traffic and dynamically process transport-layer packets from multiple controllers without requiring a dedicated cryptographic engine for every connection.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279643" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=1521%2C973&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1521" height="973" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?w=1521&amp;ssl=1 1521w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C192&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C655&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C491&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Rambus_Shared-IDE-for-PCIe-Bifurcation-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C384&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p>The solution combines high-throughput AES-GCM and SM4-GCM processing with a Shared IDE wrapper, segmented bus architecture, dynamic bandwidth allocation, and support for bifurcated PCIe configurations. Its centralized management and configurable pipeline stages simplify integration while preserving the integrity, isolation, and standards alignment required by PCIe IDE.</p>
<p>The main benefits of the solution include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Improved PPA: </strong>Shared processing reduces duplicated security hardware, with potential gate-count reductions of up to ~1.5x compared with traditional approaches.</li>
<li><strong>Better floorplanning: </strong>Security blocks can be placed independently of controllers and PHYs, reducing congestion in critical design regions.</li>
<li><strong>Bifurcation-friendly scaling: </strong>Security resource requirements do not need to increase in direct proportion to the number of protected links.</li>
<li><strong>Flexible, standards-aligned integration: </strong>Configurable deployment options support different architectures while maintaining independent protection for each port.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Looking ahead: Security architectures must scale smarter</h2>
<p>PCIe bifurcation is becoming a standard design technique because it increases flexibility and enables better utilization of available bandwidth. At the same time, IDE adoption is expanding as organizations seek stronger protection for data in motion. Unfortunately, traditional security architectures were never designed for a world where link counts grow faster than lane counts.</p>
<p>Shared IDE addresses this challenge by decoupling security scaling from controller scaling. Instead of replicating security resources every time a design introduces additional protected links, a shared architecture enables multiple interfaces to leverage common security infrastructure while preserving independent protection.</p>
<p>For SoC architects, this means lower area, reduced implementation complexity, better floorplanning flexibility, and a more scalable path to future PCIe generations. For companies building next-generation AI, cloud, networking, storage, and data center platforms, Shared IDE represents a smarter way to scale trust.</p>
<p>By combining efficient resource utilization with standards-aligned protection, the Rambus Shared IDE solution helps designers build secure bifurcated PCIe systems that are ready for the performance and connectivity demands of tomorrow.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/shared-ide-for-pcie-bifurcation-scaling-security-without-scaling-complexity-resources/">Shared IDE For PCIe Bifurcation: Scaling Security Without Scaling Complexity &#038; Resources</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<item>
		<title>How To Scale AI Arithmetic Efficiently</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Thomas Ferrere]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:05:36 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Sharpening Your Edge]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[dot product]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[floating point]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Imagination Technologies]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[matrix multiplication]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[number formats]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24279666</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Accelerating matrix multiplications in a variety of number formats while maintaining accuracy and reducing circuit area.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/">How To Scale AI Arithmetic Efficiently</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>AI workloads feature matrix multiplications in a variety of number formats, such as INT8, FP4, FP8, FP16 and BF16. Lower precision entails higher levels of acceleration. While memory bandwidth savings are immediately realized, scaling the arithmetic performance remains a challenge at lower bitwidths.</p>
<p>Imagination presents a novel approach to scaling arithmetic performance across number formats. The multiprecision dot product unit featured in the new E-Series GPUs accelerates matrix multiplications in all the above number formats. Accuracy is maintained and a third of the circuit area is saved compared to traditional design approaches using separate pipelines for each number format.</p>
<h2>So how does it work?</h2>
<p>The basic operation required to implement matrix multiplication is an accumulating dot product, of the form a0*b0 + … + a15*b15 + c = d, where a, b vectors are in lower precision and c, d are in higher precision such as FP16 or FP32. The number of terms is architecture-specific, with higher number of terms often used to reach higher performance densities. The operation is fused, such that it skips some intermediate normalization and rounding steps. By specializing the arithmetic to a given number format combination and depth of operation, higher efficiency and accuracy can be reached.</p>
<p>The explosion of number formats is one of the <a href="https://blog.imaginationtech.com/modern-trends-in-floating-point">modern trends in floating-point</a> and challenges this approach. It would lead to matrix multiplication accelerators requiring an ever-growing list of dot product hardware operators, increasing the circuit area beyond the available silicon die.</p>
<p>Format conversions may be used to share the same path for numbers of the same width, such as FP16 and BF16. However, this approach does not enable the performance to scale at lower bitwidths.</p>
<p>The need to support multiple precisions at different rates is not new. It was previously solved by SIMD vector unit implementations. In this context, a typical operation is the fused multiply-add and a 256-bits wide datapath may compute four FP64, eight FP32, or sixteen FP16 such operations in parallel. The microarchitecture of a vector unit exhibits a high level of logic reuse.</p>
<p>Vector units are, however, not well suited to mixed-precision machine learning applications, where the operations must be made more accurate by using a wider accumulation format. They also lack the performance density attainable by a fused dot product over a single format combination.</p>
<p>We built on existing techniques to target matrix multiplications and low-precision number formats. The result is a multiprecision, fused dot product unit with a vectorized datapath. It works by repurposing the multiplication and summation hardware present in an INT8 dot product to implement an efficient FP8 dot product. This involves creating additional hardware for processing the exponents and aligning the partial products, a problem specific to floating-point. The exponent processing, alignment, multiplication and summation hardware is further reused to implement accurate FP16 and BF16 dot products.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24279667" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?resize=679%2C514&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="679" height="514" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?w=679&amp;ssl=1 679w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C227&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Imagination_How-To-Scale-AI-Arithmetic-Efficiently-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C454&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 679px) 100vw, 679px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Dot product microarchitecture; processing stages with a dashed outline are for floating-point only and the low-precision hardware is reused to operate over larger widths</strong></p>
<p>Input FP8, BF16 and FP16 numbers are converted to a set of internal, normalized number formats. These new formats simplify the arithmetic implementation and ensure the precision remains constant in the presence of subnormal inputs. Products of FP8 numbers are aligned over 16 bits of precision and treated as INT8 products, while products of FP16 or BF16 are aligned over 32 bits. The products are split into two halves and summed using a shared adder structure. Dot products are then accumulated in FP32, FP16 or INT32 precision.</p>
<p>The resulting implementation is more accurate than standard methods on average, and its worst-case rounding error is bounded. The empirical accuracy was measured by simulation and compares favorably against reference models implementing floating-point summation in the working FP32 or FP16 accumulation precision. The theoretical accuracy can be analyzed using backward error analysis, which confirms rounding errors in arithmetic are small relative to expected quantization errors.</p>
<p>Vectorization enabled us to save almost a third of the circuit area, compared to a traditional design using separate pipelines for each number format to accelerate. The implementation has been formally verified end-to-end. A key element of the verification strategy was the availability of a clear, unambiguous numerical specification. This provided a platform for us to continuously optimize the design, making extensive use of vectorization techniques to maximize logic reuse.</p>
<p>This work was presented at the International Symposium on Computer Arithmetic (ARITH 2026), where the numerical analysis of AI hardware and the standardization of number formats like FP8 was a hot topic. This research contributed to the conversation on numerical aspects, and it is our hope that it will help accelerate the convergence of research models and hardware implementations towards new industry standards. For more details, please read the <a href="https://arith2026.org/papers/Vectorized%20Fused%20Dot%20Product.pdf">full paper</a> in the proceedings or <a href="https://www.imaginationtech.com/contact-us/">contact</a> our sales team to discuss our latest innovations in the field of edge AI.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-to-scale-ai-arithmetic-efficiently/">How To Scale AI Arithmetic Efficiently</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>AI: Friend And Foe For Chip Security</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/ai-friend-and-foe-for-security/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/ai-friend-and-foe-for-security/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Ed Sperling]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 07:05:17 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Special Reports]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[agentic AI]]></category>
